headline: A Paintbox Sent by Post
standfirst: For fifteen years Roger Eno sent his brother keyboard sketches, and Brian sent back the colours. The result, their first album as a duo, arrived in the very week the world fell quiet.

sections.heading: Two brothers, one room apart
paragraphs: Brothers who make music are supposed to start young, in a shared bedroom, and stay together or break apart in public. Roger and Brian Eno did neither. They grew up in Suffolk eleven years apart, with the same parents and, as Roger has put it, the same household records drifting through the house, and then went largely their own ways. Brian became the restless figure of art-rock, record production and, from 1978 and *Ambient 1: Music for Airports*, the music he called ambient. Roger, the younger, studied music at the Colchester Institute from the age of sixteen, busked in London, and ran a music therapy course at a local hospital before he ever made a record.

When he did, it was with his brother. In the early 1980s Brian and the Canadian producer Daniel Lanois were scoring *For All Mankind*, Al Reinert's documentary built from NASA's Apollo footage, and Roger joined them at Grant Avenue Studio in Hamilton, Ontario. The album that came out of those sessions, *Apollo: Atmospheres and Soundtracks*, was released in 1983, and Roger is credited as a co-writer of several of its pieces, among them "Deep Blue Day" and "Weightless". It was his first time on a record. His own debut, *Voices*, followed in 1985.

For the next three and a half decades the brothers crossed paths on film work, including David Lynch's *Dune*, but never made an album that was simply theirs. *Mixing Colours*, released by Deutsche Grammophon on 20 March 2020, is that album. It is also a strange kind of duet: two people who were almost never in the same room while making it.

sections.heading: A correspondence in MIDI
paragraphs: The record began in late 2005, without anyone deciding to begin it. Roger has a studio upstairs at home, and his habit was to climb the stairs first thing, switch everything on and improvise while still half in sleep, a state he compared to the early-morning hours Chopin is said to have favoured. Now and then he sent a sketch to Brian, simply to share what he was up to. Brian asked for something more than the recording: the MIDI file underneath it.

That request is the hinge of the whole album. MIDI does not capture a sound. It captures a performance as data: which keys were pressed, when, how hard and for how long. Hand that file to someone else and the playing survives while the instrument disappears. Brian often did not bother listening to Roger's piano version at all. He loaded the notes into his computer and asked himself what sound they wanted to be dressed in. The division of labour, as he described it, was clean: "he writes the original pieces and then I find the sound for them."

Sometimes he went further. On one piece he moved Roger's playing into a different mode, nudging every E flat up to an E. On another he ran the MIDI backwards. More often he simply listened for the mood already in the playing and coloured it in, resisting anything that would have fought it. Files went one way for years and rarely came back. When Brian did return a finished version, it might be months or years later. There were no arguments, he said, because there was no real back and forth to argue about.

Neither of them was aiming at a release. The pieces piled up over roughly fifteen years until, at someone's suggestion, they looked like a record. Roger later described the process as a long conversation and said the result was "something that neither of us could have arrived at alone."

pullQuote.text: Hand that file to someone else and the playing survives while the instrument disappears.

sections.heading: Music made on trains
paragraphs: If Roger's half of the album belongs to the early morning, Brian's belongs to the railway. "Nearly all of the work on this album was done on trains," he said, with a laptop and headphones and the English countryside sliding past the window. It is a pleasing image, and it suits the music, which has the unhurried attention of someone with nowhere else to be for the next hour.

Brian kept returning to old files on those journeys, trying them again in new clothes. The clearest proof sits in plain sight on the tracklist. [[Spring Frost]], [[Verdigris]] and [[Cerulean Blue]] all come from one MIDI performance that Roger made around 2006. Brian grouped them, loosely, as the blue ones, which is generous to the frost. Heard with that in mind, they become a small experiment in how much a sound can change a melody's meaning. The same fingers on the same keys open the album as a cold, clear morning, drift into the weathered green of oxidised copper by the middle, and return near the end under a wide, high sky.

This is what Brian meant when he talked about timbre. Orchestral instruments, he argued, are islands in a much larger sea of possible sounds, and electronic tools have filled in the water between them. He compared it to walking into a paint shop and finding thousands of new colours that have no names yet. Most of that new territory, in his view, had been explored by pop rather than by music in the classical tradition. *Mixing Colours* takes a pianist's patient, Schubertian miniatures and lets that whole new paintbox loose on them.

pullQuote.text: The same fingers on the same keys open the album as a cold, clear morning.

sections.heading: Naming the colours
paragraphs: The title was Roger's before it was the album's: "Mixing Colours" was the name of one of the pieces he had sent. The idea spread until every track carried the name of a colour, a pigment or something that has one. Roger said he has no synaesthesia and doesn't hear pitches as hues. What drew him to colour names was that they set a mood without telling a story. A title like an old road sends the mind somewhere specific. "When you have the name of a color, you have a kind of atmosphere," he explained, an atmosphere without a plot.

That is exactly how the names work while you listen. They are invitations rather than instructions, and part of the pleasure is testing them. [[Burnt Umber]] is an earth pigment, a brown that has been put in the fire, and the music is warm in that way, its colour deepened rather than brightened. [[Obsidian]] is volcanic glass, black and sharp enough to cut, and it is the darkest room in the house: a churchly organ tone, made uneasy. [[Celeste]] means heavenly, and it was the piece chosen for the album's first film.

Some names are materials rather than paints. [[Rose Quartz]] is a stone that is pink only because light passes through it. [[Quicksilver]] is mercury, a metal that refuses to hold still, and at just over five minutes the longest piece on the record. [[Cinnabar]] is the red ore that mercury is mined from, so the two sit on the tracklist like a mineral and its secret. [[Snow]] and [[Desert Sand]] are colours borrowed from weather and landscape. And [[Blonde]] is the only one named after a person's hair, which gives it an unexpected intimacy, the closest the album comes to a portrait.

sections.heading: Paintings and films
paragraphs: An album named after colours needed pictures, and it got them from close to home. The cover uses the abstract paintings of Dom Theobald, a painter who lives near Roger and has been his friend for around twenty years. Roger once wanted to give Brian one of Theobald's canvases as a present and, sensibly, told him to pick it himself. The painting Brian chose hangs in his house, and it became one of the images on the sleeve. Theobald's work, as Roger described it, is full of recognisable things like shoes, boots and chairs arranged so that you sense a story without being told it, which is a fair description of the music too.

Brian also made a series of short films for the pieces with Peter Chilvers, his long-time partner in generative software. The first, for [[Celeste]], appeared on 7 February 2020, followed by [[Blonde]] a week later and [[Slow Movement: Sand]] on 13 March, a week before the album arrived. Deutsche Grammophon marked the release itself with a midnight session streamed online.

pullQuote.text: You sense a story without being told it, which is a fair description of the music too.

sections.heading: A record for a quiet world
paragraphs: No one could have planned the timing. *Mixing Colours* came out on Friday 20 March 2020. Three days later the British prime minister told the country to stay at home, and many other countries were already doing the same. A record fifteen years in the making, built from slow piano and soft electronic light, had arrived at a moment nobody would have chosen and that suited it perfectly. It landed in kitchens and spare rooms just as people found themselves with nowhere to go.

Critics heard the coincidence immediately. In *The Observer*, Kitty Empire called it a balm for anxious times, and singled out the eerie organ of [[Obsidian]] and the way [[Wintergreen]] gathers itself into a climax that recalls Harmonia, the German group Brian once worked with, without their driving beat. On NPR, Tom Moon admitted that this kind of music could easily be waved away as spa music, then said it had become a kind of sanctuary for him during the first weeks of distancing. *The Line of Best Fit* gave it nine out of ten and saved its highest praise for the closer, [[Slow Movement: Sand]].

Not everyone was won over. *Paste* headlined its review with the complaint that the colours mostly mixed to grey, *Pitchfork* gave it 5.8 out of 10, and *Mojo* wondered whether anyone could stay engaged through seventy-five minutes of such a uniform mood. Across the reviews collected by Metacritic it averaged 72 out of 100. Listeners were less divided. By August 2020, the label reported, the album had passed twelve million streams.

The brothers answered the moment with an invitation. In a project called *A Quiet Scene*, they asked people to film a single unbroken shot of the stillness around them in lockdown: clouds, leaves moving, a bird building a nest, someone at home going about their day. 1,722 films arrived. Two hundred were shortlisted, the shortlisted film-makers voted alongside Roger and Brian, and eighteen winners, one for each track, were released one a day from 23 October to 11 November 2020.

pullQuote.text: It landed in kitchens and spare rooms just as people found themselves with nowhere to go.

sections.heading: More colours: Luminous
paragraphs: There turned out to be more paint in the box. That summer Deutsche Grammophon announced *Mixing Colours (Expanded)*, which added six new pieces and "Pewter", previously a Japan-only bonus track. Their names continue the scheme: "Moss", "Violet", "Manganese", "Vermilion", "Marble", "Pewter" and "Malachite". On 14 August 2020 the seven appeared on their own as *Luminous*, a mini-album on yellow vinyl, and on 23 October a deluxe double CD gathered all twenty-five pieces. The new titles lean towards metals and minerals, as if the brothers had moved from the paintbox to the geology shelf.

sections.heading: How to listen to colour
paragraphs: In his notes for *Music for Airports*, Brian described wanting music that would bring calm and room to think, and *Mixing Colours* is often taken in that spirit, as background. It works as background. But it rewards the other kind of listening too, and the method of its making tells you how. Every piece is a real performance, with all the small hesitations and leanings of a person at a keyboard in the early morning, set inside a sound chosen by someone else on a train. Underneath the haze there is always a hand.

Roger said he wanted the music released because it has staying power: the longer you spend with it, the more you can walk into the landscape and remain there. Brian added that the emotional weather of each piece was set by Roger's playing, and that his own job was to paint it in rather than to overrule it. You can hear both halves if you choose to. Follow the melody in [[Dark Sienna]] or [[Iris]] and you are listening to Roger's nineteenth-century sympathies. Follow the air around the notes in [[Ultramarine]] or [[Deep Saffron]] and you are listening to Brian's paint shop of nameless colours.

The last word belongs to the title that reads least like the others. [[Slow Movement: Sand]] borrows the language of the concert hall, the slow movement of a sonata or symphony, and pairs it with the most ordinary of materials, something that only exists because time has worn other things down. It is a fitting end for a record that took fifteen years, made by two brothers who hardly discussed it while they made it, and that arrived in the world on the very week the world went quiet enough to hear it.

pullQuote.text: Underneath the haze there is always a hand.
